newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Pol Pot trial could rock Cambodian politics.
newsitem.headline: Pol Pot trial could rock Cambodian politics.

text.p: Khmer Rouge chief Pol Pot might be a sick old man, broken and betrayed by his own guerrilla army, but he could still rock Cambodian politics if brought to trial, analysts said on Monday.

Cambodia's two prime ministers, both of whom have at different times sided with Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge, said last week in a rare display of public unity that he should face an international tribunal to answer for his crimes.

There have been conflicting reports of Pol Pot's recent whereabouts but a government general on Sunday said was being detained at the jungle headquarters of a breakaway faction of the Khmer Rouge which captured him last week.
General Nhiek Bun Chhay, who said he had met Pol Pot on Sunday, said he would be handed over to the government soon.
But Ranariddh on Monday said there were people in Cambodia who never wanted to see Pol Pot stand trial because of the fear they could be implicated in his crimes.

There are few political players in Cambodia, from King Norodom Sihanouk and Ranariddh on down, who have not at some time been allied with the man under whose 1975-79 "killing fields" reign of terror more than a million Cambodians died.
"All of them have been linked to him at one time or another," said a diplomat. "I think many people in Cambodia would have some problems."
"Pol Pot didn't kill everyone himself," said an analyst of the Khmer Rouge. "Maybe he never killed anyone. He had other people do it for him.
"Most likely there are a significant number of people, maybe now living quietly, who would be found guilty of crimes against humanity if they were ever brought to trial."
Many Cambodian politicians, including Co-Premier Hun Sen, were former Khmer Rouge members who broke with Pol Pot during his rule.
"There are former Khmer Rouge who are in the government," said Lao Mong Hay, director of the Khmer Institute of Democracy. "I think some might not like to be exposed.
"But if Pol Pot can be brought to stand trial, let him speak and let the others defend themselves," he said.
Last week the two prime ministers sent a joint letter to the secretary general of the United Nations to ask for the world body's help in bringing to justice those responsible for the slaughter.

The United States has also called for 69-year-old Pol Pot to be brought before an international tribunal. The New York Times said on Monday that the United States had asked Canada to help extradite Pol Pot as Canada had a law against genocide.
Political analysts said if Pol Pot were ever arrested it was important that he be tried by an international court.
"The Cambodian courts are not independent. There's no chance he'd get a fair trial and it wouldn't serve the purposes of getting to the truth of what happened," said one analyst.
"The important thing is that the choice of who gets tried is put outside the political sphere, that the international community gets the right to decide," the analyst said.
"Trying him here would be more divisive than healing," said another diplomat.
Pol Pot and his Khmer Rouge have had links across the political spectrum over the last three decades of strife.
King Sihanouk allied himself with the guerrillas he had earlier dubbed "les Khmer Rouges" after he was overthrown in a rightwing coup in 1970.
Sihanouk again formed an alliance with them after Vietnamese forces invaded Cambodia and overthrew Pol Pot's government in 1979.
Ranariddh was the leader of the royalist forces who fought alongside the Khmer Rouge against Vietnam's army of occupation and the Hanoi-backed government in the 1980s.

Hun Sen joined the Khmer Rouge in the early 1970s. Wounded in fighting as the guerrillas closed in on Phnom Penh in 1975, he went on to become a mid-ranking military commander in eastern Cambodia but broke with the Khmer Rouge and fled to Vietnam in 1977.
Some 18 months later Hun Sen returned to Cambodia with a Vietnamese army of occupation and began his climb to the top.
Many senior members of his Cambodian People's Party were at one-time members of the Khmer Rouge.
More than a million people were executed as enemies of Pol Pot's agrarian revolution or died of disease, starvation, torture or overwork.
